draft.title: Register and diction
card: How formal or informal the language is. A letter to a principal uses a formal register. A text to a friend uses an informal one.
The particular words a writer chooses. Words with a similar meaning can feel very different, such as "child" and "kid", or "purchase" and "grab".
Slang, contractions and short sentences often suggest an informal register. Longer sentences and precise, technical words often suggest a formal one.
Both signal the writer's relationship with the reader. Formal language keeps some distance and shows respect. Informal language feels close and friendly.
draft.remember: Register is the level of formality. Diction is the word choice that creates it.

a.q: Which sentence is written in the most formal register?
opts: Residents are requested to refrain from parking here
Please don't park here, folks
Park somewhere else, mate
No parking here, thanks heaps
a.why: Requested and refrain from are precise, formal word choices, and the sentence keeps a distance from the reader. The other three use contractions, slang or casual phrases, which make the tone closer and more informal.
a.clue: Look for the sentence with no slang or contractions.

b.q: Zoe writes a speech for her Year 11 class. She says, "Mate, we've smashed this term." What do her diction and register mainly show about her relationship with the audience?
opts: It is close and relaxed, as she is speaking to peers
It is distant and respectful, as she is speaking to a judge
It is hostile, because she uses the word smashed
It is neutral, because the sentence is so short
b.why: Mate, the contraction we've and the casual word smashed make the register informal, which suggests she feels close to her classmates. Smashed is slang for achieved well, so it does not suggest hostility.
b.clue: Think about who would be spoken to this way.

a.best: Residents are requested to refrain from parking here

b.best: It is close and relaxed, as she is speaking to peers

problems.detail: The remember line says diction is the word choice that 'creates' register. That makes register depend on diction alone, which is neater than the card. The card says sentence length and contractions also signal register.

'purchase' and 'grab' are not a clear pair of words with a similar meaning. 'Grab' mainly means to seize and only means 'buy' in casual phrases. 'Buy' and 'purchase' would show the idea without confusion.
The distractor 'speaking to a judge' contradicts the stem, which says she speaks to her Year 11 class. That makes the question very easy to eliminate for Year 11.

check.summary: Both questions have one clear right answer. The remember line oversimplifies by saying diction alone creates register, the 'purchase'/'grab' pair is a weak example of near-synonyms, and question b has a distractor that contradicts its own stem.

a.q: Which sentence is written in the most formal register?
opts: Residents are requested to refrain from parking here
Please don't park here, folks, we need the space
Park somewhere else, mate, this spot's taken
No parking here, thanks heaps for helping out
a.why: Requested and refrain from are precise, formal word choices, and the sentence keeps a distance from the reader. The other three use contractions, slang or casual phrases, which make the tone closer and more informal.
a.clue: Look for the sentence with no slang or contractions.

b.q: Zoe writes a speech for her Year 11 class. She says, "Mate, we've smashed this term." What do her diction and register mainly show about her relationship with the audience?
opts: It is close and relaxed, as she is speaking to peers
It is distant and respectful, as a speech is a formal text
It is hostile, because she uses the word smashed
It is neutral, because the sentence is so short
b.why: Mate, the contraction we've and the casual word smashed make the register informal, which suggests she feels close to her classmates. Speeches can be formal, but the register comes from the words she actually uses, and these are informal.
b.clue: Judge by her words, not by the type of text.
